#### 1. short stature, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal anomalies with or without cardiac anomalies 1  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.417)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2129379)

**Proposed mechanism:** EFEMP2 (HGNC:3002) —DISRUPTS→ Extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198); Extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198) —LEADS_TO→ Short stature (HP:0004308); Extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198) —LEADS_TO→ Facial dysmorphism (HP:0001949); Extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198) —LEADS_TO→ Skeletal anomalies (HP:0002670); BMP2 (HGNC:1407) —DISRUPTS→ Connective tissue development (GO:0048760); Connective tissue development (GO:0048760) —LEADS_TO→ Short stature (HP:0004308); Connective tissue development (GO:0048760) —LEADS_TO→ Facial dysmorphism (HP:0001949); Connective tissue development (GO:0048760) —LEADS_TO→ Skeletal anomalies (HP:0002670); Connective tissue development (GO:0048760) —LEADS_TO→ Cardiac anomaly (HP:0001627). Loss-of-function mutations in EFEMP2 disrupt extracellular matrix organization, leading to short stature, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal anomalies (Disease A). Similarly, loss-of-function mutations in BMP2 disrupt connective tissue development, also contributing to short stature, facial dysmorphism, skeletal anomalies, and potentially cardiac anomalies (Disease B). The shared convergence on the broad pathways of extracellular matrix organization and connective tissue development, which are intimately related and involve common downstream phenotypic manifestations, forms the mechanistic link.

**How to falsify it:** If pathogenic variants in EFEMP2 are found to be common (>1% allele frequency) in control populations (e.g., gnomAD) or if experimental studies show no functional overlap between EFEMP2 and BMP2 in connective tissue and extracellular matrix regulation, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: rs727560504)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanistic basis in extracellular matrix and connective tissue regulation could lead to the development of common therapeutic strategies targeting these pathways for both diseases, potentially improving outcomes for patients with short stature, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal anomalies.
